title: What is GitOps — using Git as the single source of truth for infrastructure and application deployment; a GitOps operator (ArgoCD/Flux) watches the Git repo and automatically syncs the cluster to match what is in Git — and why is it better than manual `kubectl apply` (auditable, repeatable, self-healing)?
shortTitle: What GitOps is and why it is better than manual kubectl apply

s1_definition.profdef: GitOps is an operational model in which the desired state of your infrastructure and applications is declared in a Git repository that serves as the single source of truth, and an in-cluster GitOps operator such as ArgoCD or Flux continuously watches that repository and automatically reconciles the live cluster to match it. Because every change is a Git commit, deployments become auditable, repeatable, and self-healing: the history shows who changed what and when, the same commit reproduces the same environment, and the operator corrects any drift by reverting the cluster back to the declared state.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India keeps one official, version-controlled rulebook describing exactly how every branch should be set up — counters, signage, safe configuration. Instead of a manager walking into each branch and changing things by hand (and nobody knowing who changed what), the bank employs a diligent inspector who constantly compares each branch to the official rulebook and quietly fixes anything that does not match. To change a branch, you do not touch the branch directly; you edit the rulebook, it is reviewed and approved, and the inspector rolls the change out everywhere. Every edit to the rulebook is signed and dated, so there is a perfect audit trail.
s1_definition.oneliner: GitOps makes Git the single source of truth and lets an operator continuously sync the cluster to match it, giving auditable, repeatable, self-healing deployments that manual kubectl apply cannot.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** GitOps is an operational model in which the desired state of your infrastructure and applications is declared in a Git repository that serves as the single source of truth, and an in-cluster GitOps operator such as ArgoCD or Flux continuously watches that repository and automatically reconciles the live cluster to match it. Because every change is a Git commit, deployments become auditable, repeatable, and self-healing: the history shows who changed what and when, the same commit reproduces the same environment, and the operator corrects any drift by reverting the cluster back to the declared state.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India keeps one official, version-controlled rulebook describing exactly how every branch should be set up — counters, signage, safe configuration. Instead of a manager walking into each branch and changing things by hand (and nobody knowing who changed what), the bank employs a diligent inspector who constantly compares each branch to the official rulebook and quietly fixes anything that does not match. To change a branch, you do not touch the branch directly; you edit the rulebook, it is reviewed and approved, and the inspector rolls the change out everywhere. Every edit to the rulebook is signed and dated, so there is a perfect audit trail.

**One line to remember:** GitOps makes Git the single source of truth and lets an operator continuously sync the cluster to match it, giving auditable, repeatable, self-healing deployments that manual kubectl apply cannot.

sections.s2_technical:
In GitOps the desired state lives as declarative manifests in Git — Kubernetes YAML, Helm charts, or Kustomize overlays — describing exactly what should run: which Deployments, how many replicas, which image tags, which config. Nothing is changed by hand on the cluster. To deploy, you open a pull request that edits those files; after review and merge, the change is in Git. A GitOps operator running inside the cluster, such as ArgoCD or Flux, watches the repository and compares the declared state to the actual cluster state, a process called reconciliation. When it detects a difference, it applies the manifests to bring the cluster into line, and it keeps doing this on a loop forever.

This is better than manual kubectl apply on several concrete axes. First, auditability: with GitOps every change is a Git commit with an author, a timestamp, a message, and usually a reviewed pull request, so you have a complete, tamper-evident record of who changed what and why — which is essential for a regulated bank. With manual kubectl apply, someone runs a command from their laptop and there is often no durable record of what was applied or by whom. Second, repeatability: because the entire desired state is in Git, you can recreate an identical environment — a new region, a disaster-recovery cluster, or a rebuilt cluster — by pointing the operator at the same commit, and you get exactly the same result. Manual apply depends on whatever sequence of commands a person happened to run, which is hard to reproduce faithfully.

Third, self-healing through drift correction: the operator continuously compares live state to Git, so if someone manually edits a resource, or a controller or a crash changes something, the operator detects the drift and reverts the cluster back to the declared state automatically. Manual kubectl apply has no such guard — once applied, nothing watches for drift, so the cluster silently diverges from what anyone intended. Fourth, easy rollback: rolling back is just reverting the Git commit, after which the operator syncs the cluster back to the previous good state, which is far safer and clearer than trying to remember and re-apply old manifests by hand. Fifth, access and security: engineers do not need broad direct cluster credentials, because they change the system through Git and the operator holds the privileged access, which shrinks the blast radius and centralizes control.

A senior nuance is the separation of continuous integration from continuous deployment: CI builds and tests the image and may update the image tag in the Git repo, and then the GitOps operator handles deployment by syncing — this is a pull-based model where the cluster pulls its desired state from Git, as opposed to a push-based model where a CI server like Jenkins pushes changes into the cluster with credentials. Pull-based GitOps is generally more secure and more resilient because the cluster reaches out to Git rather than exposing deploy credentials to an external system. The overall effect is that deployments become a reviewed, reproducible, continuously-enforced declaration rather than a series of imperative, unlogged commands.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India runs its transfer service on Kubernetes. Previously engineers ran kubectl apply by hand, which caused untracked changes, drift, and painful rollbacks. We want to demonstrate GitOps: a Git repository holds the desired state, and an operator reconciles the cluster to match, correcting drift automatically.

Problem 1 — Manual changes left no audit trail, and nobody could say who scaled the transfer service or changed its image. In GitOps every change is a committed, reviewed desired state, so the history is the audit.

Problem 2 — Someone manually edited a live Deployment, causing drift from intent. A GitOps operator detects drift and reverts the cluster to the declared state, which is self-healing.

Problem 3 — Rollback was error-prone. In GitOps rollback is reverting a commit and letting the operator sync. Our runnable Java simulation models a `GitRepo` holding desired state, a `Cluster` holding live state, and a `GitOpsOperator` that reconciles on a loop, detecting and correcting drift and supporting rollback by reverting the desired state. Classes: `DesiredState`, `GitRepo`, `Cluster`, `GitOpsOperator`, and a `GitOpsDemo` main. Real ArgoCD YAML is shown as reference.

##### 4c. GitOps Configuration (YAML in Git)

```yaml
# ─── File: gitops-repo/transfer-service-deployment.yaml ───
# Desired state — the ONLY place this is changed is via a reviewed Git PR.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: transfer-service
  namespace: banking
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: transfer-service }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: transfer-service }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: transfer-service
          image: registry.nbi.in/transfer-service:4.2.0    # pinned image tag
          ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
```

```yaml
# ─── File: gitops-repo/argocd-application.yaml ───
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: transfer-service
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: banking
  source:
    repoURL: https://git.nbi.in/platform/gitops-repo.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: .
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: banking
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true          # delete resources removed from Git
      selfHeal: true       # revert manual drift back to Git state
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Run the Java simulation
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -cp target/classes com.bank.gitops.GitOpsDemo

# Real GitOps workflow (ArgoCD)
kubectl apply -f gitops-repo/argocd-application.yaml   # register the app once
# Thereafter: NEVER kubectl apply the Deployment by hand.
git commit -am "deploy v4.3.0" && git push             # ArgoCD auto-syncs
argocd app get transfer-service                        # view sync + health
argocd app rollback transfer-service <prev-revision>   # or just git revert
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a Git repository and a cluster both starting at transfer-service version 4.2.0 with three replicas.

Step 1 — The operator reconciles and finds the desired state in Git equals the live cluster state, so it does nothing and logs that it is in sync.

Step 2 — Someone runs kubectl edit by hand and scales the service down to one replica, creating drift. On the next reconcile the operator detects that live state (one replica) differs from Git (three replicas), and because self-heal is on, it reapplies the Git desired state, restoring three replicas automatically — this is the self-healing property.

Step 3 — To deploy version 4.3.0 the GitOps way, Priya commits a change to the repository through a reviewed pull request. The operator reconciles, sees the new image in Git, and rolls it out to the cluster — no one ran kubectl apply.

Step 4 — Version 4.3.0 shows a latency regression, so rollback is simply reverting the commit back to 4.2.0. The operator reconciles and restores 4.2.0 on the cluster.

Step 5 — The Git history now contains every change with author and message, which is the complete audit trail: who deployed, who rolled back, and why — something manual kubectl apply never produced.

Final output:

```

2026-10-30 02:40:00 [INFO   ] === Someone edits the cluster by hand (drift) ===

2026-10-30 02:40:00 [WARNING] OUT OF SYNC — desired=image=transfer-service:4.2.0, replicas=3 live=image=transfer-service:4.2.0, replicas=1
2026-10-30 02:40:00 [INFO   ] CLUSTER apply → image=transfer-service:4.2.0, replicas=3
2026-10-30 02:40:00 [INFO   ] Self-healed cluster back to Git desired state.
2026-10-30 02:40:00 [INFO   ] GIT COMMIT by priya — deploy v4.3.0 (PR #214 reviewed) → image=transfer-service:4.3.0, replicas=3
2026-10-30 02:40:00 [INFO   ] CLUSTER apply → image=transfer-service:4.3.0, replicas=3
2026-10-30 02:40:00 [INFO   ] GIT COMMIT by priya — revert to v4.2.0 (PR #215, latency regression) → image=transfer-service:4.2.0, replicas=3

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Engineer edits manifest → Pull Request → review → merge to Git (main)
    │                                                    │
    │  (Git = SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH, full audit)        │
    ▼                                                    ▼
  GitOpsOperator (ArgoCD/Flux) in cluster — reconcile loop
    │ compare desired(Git) vs live(cluster)
    │
    ├─ in sync    → do nothing
    ├─ drift      → re-apply Git state (SELF-HEAL)
    ├─ new commit → roll out new image/replicas
    └─ reverted   → restore previous state (ROLLBACK = git revert)
    │
    ▼
  Cluster live state === Git desired state (continuously enforced)
```

  └───────┬────────┘        └────────┬────────┘
          │ reads                    │ writes
          └───────────┬──────────────┘
                      ▼
          ┌──────────────────────────┐   compares  ┌──────────────┐
          │   GitOpsOperator         │────────────▶│ DesiredState  │

          │ + reconcile(): boolean   │             │ + equals()    │
          └──────────────────────────┘             └──────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Reconciliation ─────────────────────────────────

  [IN_SYNC] ─drift / new commit─→ [OUT_OF_SYNC] ─selfHeal/apply─→ [IN_SYNC]
                                        │ selfHeal off
                                        ▼
                                   [DRIFTED] (undesirable)

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. GitOpsDemo.main()
  2.   → operator.reconcile() → in sync, no-op
  3.   → cluster.manualEdit(replicas=1) → drift
  4.   → operator.reconcile() → detect drift → cluster.apply(Git state) [self-heal]

  6.   → repo.update(v4.2.0 revert) → operator.reconcile() → rollback
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
GitOps is an operational model where the desired state of my infrastructure and applications is declared in a Git repository that is the single source of truth, and an in-cluster operator such as ArgoCD or Flux continuously watches that repository and reconciles the live cluster to match it. Nothing is changed on the cluster by hand; to deploy, I open a pull request that edits the declarative manifests, and after review and merge the operator detects the change and applies it. Because every change is a Git commit, the whole system becomes auditable, repeatable, and self-healing.

It is better than manual kubectl apply on several concrete axes. On auditability, every change has an author, timestamp, message, and reviewed pull request, giving a complete, tamper-evident record of who changed what and why, which is essential in a regulated bank; manual apply from someone's laptop leaves no durable record. On repeatability, because the entire desired state is in Git, I can recreate an identical environment — a disaster-recovery cluster or a new region — just by pointing the operator at the same commit, whereas manual apply depends on whatever commands a person happened to run. On self-healing, the operator continuously compares live state to Git, so if someone edits a resource by hand or a crash changes something, it detects the drift and reverts the cluster to the declared state automatically; manual apply has no such guard and the cluster silently diverges. And rollback becomes trivial and safe: I simply revert the Git commit and the operator syncs the cluster back to the previous good state.

In my project at the National Bank of India we moved the transfer service to GitOps with ArgoCD, and the difference was immediate. When someone scaled the service down by hand, the operator detected the drift and restored the declared replica count on its own. Deploying a new version was a reviewed pull request that bumped the image tag, and when that version showed a latency regression, rolling back was just reverting the commit. A senior point I always add is that GitOps is pull-based — the cluster pulls its desired state from Git rather than a CI server pushing in with credentials — which is more secure and resilient because engineers never need broad direct cluster access; the operator holds the privileged access and Git holds the truth. That is why GitOps turns deployment from a series of imperative, unlogged commands into a reviewed, reproducible, continuously-enforced declaration.
